  Maladaptive Strategies: Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Amara was thirty-four when armed men entered the compound where she worked as a nurse in a rural clinic in South Sudan. That was eight years ago. She had been checking supplies in the back room when the shooting started—a sound she would come to know in her body before her mind could name it. The men separated the staff. What happened over the next hours existed in her memory as something both vivid and impossible, a sequence of violence and humiliation so extreme that even now, sitting in the therapist's office, she could come to believe it had occurred to her. Sometimes she wondered if the memory belonged to someone else entirely, a story she had absorbed rather than lived. Yet her body knew. Her body remembered with perfect, treacherous clarity.

When she finally escaped the country two years later, she carried that memory like a second skeleton. She had moved to the United States, and the work she found—assembling medical components at a factory in a sprawling industrial park outside the city—was nothing like the nursing she had trained for. The factory floor was loud and predictable in ways that felt safe at first. She could control the rhythm of it, the repetitive motions, the hiss of machinery at regular intervals. But the irony was not lost on her: she was back around medical equipment, the very instruments that had once defined her as a healer, now reduced to anonymous parts moving along a conveyor belt. It was a different form of work entirely, one that required no presence of mind, no decision-making, no responsibility for anyone's life but her own. In some ways, that was exactly what she needed.

The first year in America, Amara had tried to live normally. She wore her old clothes, the bright fabrics she loved—indigo and crimson kente cloth that her mother had sent from Ghana. But in the spring, when the weather turned warm and humid, matching the season when she had been taken, her body had begun to betray her. The smell of rain on hot earth—a smell that had been present that day—would arrive on the breeze, and suddenly she could not breathe. She had stopped wearing the clothes associated with that time. She had stopped going outside when the weather felt similar. Gradually, she had narrowed the world. At home, she listened. Always listening. For footsteps on the stairs, for the sound of a key in the lock, for voices that might indicate someone was coming. Her apartment was on the second floor, and she had memorized every creak of the building, every sound that meant safety and every sound that meant danger. When her ex-husband had tried to visit last year—a man named Kofi—she had felt her entire body tense, flooded with a fear that made no logical sense. He was not one of them. But her body did not distinguish. Her body reacted to danger before her mind could catch up, before she could remind herself that she was safe, that this was America, that it was only a name.

At the factory, her supervisor had begun to notice the changes. She had taken to wearing heavy makeup, layers of it, as though she could paint over what had happened to her skin, make herself unrecognizable even to herself. When he asked if she was all right, she had said yes. She had not mentioned that she flinched at every unexpected sound, that her coworkers had begun to notice how she startled at the normal noises of the production line—the pneumatic hiss of machinery, the clang of metal on metal. She had not mentioned that she had stopped attending the evening shifts because darkness made the listening worse, and she had been quietly demoted to day work, a consequence no one discussed but everyone understood. The demotion meant less pay, fewer hours, less stability. It meant she had to rely more heavily on her sister for help with rent. It meant she was no longer the independent woman she had been.

What frightened Amara most was that her body no longer felt like her own. She could not trust it to react appropriately, to distinguish between real danger and the ghosts of danger. She was no longer capable of the things that had once defined her—the steadiness, the presence of mind, the ability to help others without falling apart. The world had shown itself to be a place where men could take what they wanted, and no amount of vigilance could prevent that. She was forty-two now, and she had come to believe that she would spend the rest of her life listening for footsteps, jumping at sounds, trying to paint over the past with makeup and mental distraction. Last month, her sister had finally convinced her to call someone. She had made the appointment. She was here. And what she was most afraid of, more than anything, was that this was simply who she was now—that the nurse she had been, the woman who had once run toward people in crisis, was gone forever.
